opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it is that you can't fully prepare for it in advance. You build the muscle by doing it. But a few things have helped me.

One is my background in math competitions and research. In a competition you have limited time, an incomplete picture, and you have to commit to an approach. If it isn't working, you need to notice that quickly and switch. That's surprisingly close to what founders do every day. You rarely have complete information, and waiting for certainty is itself a decision, usually a bad one.

The second thing is separating reversible decisions from irreversible ones. Most decisions in a startup are reversible: which experiment to run this week, how to phrase a job post, which customer conversation to prioritize. For those I try to move very fast and accept that some will be wrong. Then there's a small set that are really hard to undo, like who you hire early, what your core technical bet is, and who you raise money from. Those deserve slowing down, sleeping on it, and talking to people I trust. A lot of the stress goes away once you realize not everything needs the same level of agonizing.

Third, I rely on the team. I don't think a founder should be the bottleneck on every call. If you hire people who are much better than you in their areas and you trust them, a lot of fast decisions can happen without you. My job becomes setting the direction clearly enough that people can make good calls on their own.

On the emotional side, I try to stay grounded in why we're doing this. For us that's building AI that can actually reason mathematically, which I find genuinely exciting. When the pressure is high, coming back to the mission helps a lot. It turns a stressful day into one small step in a long journey rather than a crisis.

And honestly, sleep and exercise matter. It sounds boring, but your decision quality drops a lot when you're exhausted, and as a founder your judgment is one of the most important resources the company has. So I try to protect it.

r001.rationale: The response says founders build the decision-making muscle by doing it, repeatedly committing to an approach with incomplete information and switching when needed.

r002.rationale: It says founders rarely have complete information and that waiting for certainty is itself a decision, so they must act before their information feels sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you can't fully prepare for it, and anyone who tells you they walked in ready is either lucky or not remembering accurately. But there are things that helped me.

The first is that I came from a math background, and math trains you in a very specific way. You spend years working on problems where you don't know if there's even an answer, and you learn to be comfortable sitting in that uncertainty without panicking. That turned out to be weirdly transferable. A lot of founder decisions aren't actually hard because the analysis is hard. They're hard because you have to act before the analysis is finished. Math gave me some tolerance for making a move with incomplete information and then updating when the next piece of evidence arrives.

The second thing is separating the decisions that are reversible from the ones that aren't. Most of what feels high-pressure in a given week is actually reversible. You hire someone, it doesn't work, you fix it. You ship a feature, users hate it, you pull it. For those, I try to decide fast and not agonize, because the cost of delay is usually higher than the cost of being wrong. The ones that are genuinely one-way doors, like who your cofounders are or what problem you're fundamentally betting the company on, I slow down a lot and I talk to people who disagree with me.

And then the third thing, which I underestimated, is just physical. Sleep, exercise, having one or two people outside the company you can be completely honest with. When I'm running on no sleep, every decision feels existential, and that's not a signal about the decision, it's a signal about me. So I've learned to notice when the pressure I'm feeling is real versus manufactured by exhaustion. It sounds unglamorous, but I think taking care of the instrument that's making the decisions is probably the highest-leverage preparation there is.

r001.rationale: The response describes gaining tolerance for decisions with incomplete information through a math background, but does not present repeatedly taking leaps of faith as a practice for building that capacity.

r002.rationale: It says founder decisions often require acting before analysis is finished and describes making moves with incomplete information.

astra-6.text:
I think of preparation less as rehearsing every possible scenario and more as building the ability to think clearly when you don’t have all the information. You can always find another question to investigate, but as a founder, you still have to decide.

One useful distinction is whether a decision is reversible. If it is, you can often move quickly, try something, and learn. If it’s difficult to reverse, then it deserves more time and more input. That helps you avoid treating every decision as equally high stakes.

And I think you build that judgment through practice: taking responsibility, making a call, and then honestly looking at what happened. Was your reasoning sound? What did you miss? A good outcome doesn’t necessarily mean you made a good decision, and a bad outcome doesn’t necessarily mean you made a bad one.

The other part is knowing yourself under stress. When do you become reactive? When do you hesitate too long? For me, the goal would be to create enough space between feeling pressure and acting on it that the pressure doesn’t make the decision for you.

r001.rationale: It recommends practicing judgment by taking responsibility and making calls, but does not present repeatedly taking leaps of faith as building a habitual capacity for founding pressure.

r002.rationale: It says founders still have to decide even when they lack all the information, despite being able to investigate further.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it less as preparing for one big, high-pressure moment and more as building the habit of making decisions when you don’t have all the information. You can always find another question to ask or another thing to analyze. At some point, you have to decide what you know, what you’re assuming, and what would make you change your mind.

It helps to distinguish decisions you can reverse from decisions that are harder to undo. For the reversible ones, you can move quickly and learn. For the consequential ones, you want to slow down enough to get the right input, even if you’re under pressure.

And there’s an emotional component: being able to feel uncertainty without immediately trying to make it disappear. The goal isn’t to feel completely confident every time. It’s to make a thoughtful choice, take responsibility for it, and stay willing to update.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a habit of deciding without complete information, but does not present repeatedly taking leaps of faith as the way to build that capacity.

r002.rationale: It says founders must decide when they lack all the information and may feel there is always more to analyze, including while under pressure.
